'''Leendert Ginjaar''' (28 May 1928 – 17 September 2003) was a Dutch politician of the [[People's Party for Freedom and Democracy]] (VVD) and chemist.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.absolutefacts.nl/politiek/data/ginjaarl1928.htm|title=Leendert Ginjaar (1928-2003)|publisher=Absolutefacts.nl|date=15 May 2012|accessdate=9 December 2018|language=nl}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Ginjaar attended a [[Gymnasium (school)|Gymnasium]] in [[Leiden]] from April 1940 until May 1946 and applied at the [[Leiden University]] in June 1946 [[Major (academic)|majoring]] in [[Chemistry]] and obtaining a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in June 1948 before graduating with a [[Master of Science]] degree in July 1952 and worked as a researcher at the Leiden University before he got a [[doctorate]] as a [[Doctor of Science]] in Chemistry in August 1956. Ginjaar worked as a researcher at the [[Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research|Organisation for Applied Scientific Research]] from August 1956 until December 1977 and served as Director of the department of Climatology from February 1970 until December 1977. Ginjaar served on the [[States-provincial|Provincial-Council]] of [[South Holland]] from July 1971 until December 1977. Ginjaar also served as a [[Scientific Council for Government Policy|Member of the Scientific Council for Government Policy]] from 1 July 1973 until 19 December 1977.

After the [[1977 Dutch general election|election of 1977]] Ginjaar was appointed as [[List of Ministers of Health of the Netherlands|Minister of Health and Environment]] in the [[First Van Agt cabinet|Cabinet Van Agt-Wiegel]], taking office on 19 December 1977. Ginjaar served as acting [[List of Ministers of Education of the Netherlands#List of Ministers without Portfolio|Minister for Science Policy]] from 1 April 1979 until 3 May 1979 following the death of [[Rinus Peijnenburg]]. In December 1980, Ginjaar announced that he wouldn't stand for the [[1981 Dutch general election|election of 1981]] but wanted to run for the Senate. Ginjaar was elected as a [[Senate (Netherlands)|Member of the Senate]] after the [[Historic composition of the Senate of the Netherlands|Senate election of 1981]], taking office on 25 August 1981 serving as a [[frontbencher]] chairing the parliamentary committee for Higher Education and Science Policy and the parliamentary committee for Housing and Spatial Planning and [[spokesperson]] for [[Ministry of Housing, Spatial Planning and the Environment (Netherlands)|the Environment]], Higher Education and [[Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality|Agriculture]]. The Cabinet Van Agt–Wiegel was replaced by the [[Second Van Agt cabinet|Cabinet Van Agt II]] following the [[1981 Dutch cabinet formation|cabinet formation of 1981]] on 11 September 1981. Ginjaar also served as [[Chair of the People's Party for Freedom and Democracy|Chairmen of the People's Party for Freedom and Democracy]] from 29 November 1986 until 4 October 1991. Ginjaar served as a distinguished professor of [[Medical ethics]] at the [[Utrecht University]] from 1 September 1982 until 1 January 1986 and also served as Chairman of the [[Board of education|Education board]] of the Utrecht University from 10 September 1982 until 1 January 1986 and a distinguished professor of [[Climatology]] and [[Medical research]] at the [[Maastricht University|State University of Limburg]] from 1 March 1990 until 1 September 1994. Ginjaar was selected as [[Parliamentary leader]] of the People's Party for Freedom and Democracy in the Senate following the election of [[Frits Korthals Altes]] as [[President of the Senate (Netherlands)|President of the Senate]], serving from 11 March 1997 until 14 September 1999. In November 2002 Ginjaar announced his retirement from national politics and that he wouldn't stand for the [[2003 Dutch Senate election|Senate election of 2003]] and continued to serve until the end of the parliamentary term on 10 June 2003.

Ginjaar was known for his abilities as a [[Management|manager]] and ''[[wikt:policy wonk|policy wonk]]''. Ginjaar continued to comment on political affairs until his death four months later at the age of 75. His wife [[Nell Ginjaar-Maas|Nell]] was also a politician who served as [[List of Ministers of Education of the Netherlands#List of State Secretaries for Education|State Secretary for Education and Sciences]] from 5 November 1982 until 7 November 1989.
